evidence_boundary: Analyst extraction from captured D3 PDF text; these fields improve evaluation specificity but remain author-reported and are not independent reproduction.

records.eval: COMSOL frequency-domain pressure-acoustics simulations vary tracheal length, glottis radius, and beak angle; simulated resonance peaks are compared with house-sparrow and domestic-canary vocalizations. The reported comparison is spectral/formant frequency and SPL behavior, not a human-listener denominator.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 2.1–3.2: 1,847 CT slices; 10°/20° beak configurations; resonance peaks at 5.2/6.0 kHz for the biphonic model and comparison with measured vocalizations.

records.eval: Evaluation uses ESD, Expresso, and LibriTTS test sets. Objective measures are Whisper-Large-3 WER, Resemblyzer speaker-embedding cosine similarity, Emotion2Vec+ emotion similarity and classification accuracy, and speaker-verification EER; subjective measures are 1–5 naturalness, speaker-similarity, and emotion MOS from 15 users with 10–15 samples per model.
records.evaluation_source: Section 4.1: dataset-specific source/target conditions, objective metrics, subjective protocol, and tested sample scope.

records.eval: The study transcodes 2,061,600 VoxForge files and 75,600 DARPA-TIMIT files through PSTN, VoIP, and neural codecs at specified bitrates, then computes ViSQOL speech-mode quality. Language effects are analyzed across 17 languages and gender effects on TIMIT metadata; codec/bitrate and subgroup are the denominators.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 2.2–2.3: codec paths, bitrates, file counts, ViSQOL metric, and VoxForge/TIMIT subgroup design.

records.eval: The ML-SUPERB 2.0 development and dialect-development sets evaluate language-identification accuracy and character error rate across the challenge languages, dialects, and accents. Uniform interpolation of the embedding and generative LID models is compared with each component; the reported reductions are 31% on the regular development set and 23% on the dialectal set.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3–4.1 and Tables 2–3: 141/153-language public coverage, 56 dialects/accents, LID/CER metrics, and development-set denominators.

records.eval: The analysis uses 4,056 /s/ tokens from 42 Nigerian English speakers across Hausa, Igbo, and Yoruba groups. CoG, duration, skewness, and zero-crossing measures are analyzed with mixed-effects regressions using gender, birth year, segment duration, speaker, and phonological environment; reported effects are group- and predictor-specific rather than a recognition accuracy score.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 2.1–2.3 and 3.1: corpus/token counts, acoustic measures, model structure, and reported fixed/random effects.

records.eval: Thirty-two Tokyo Japanese listeners perform a 96-trial cross-modal lexical-decision experiment with congruent, prosodically mispronounced, segmentally mispronounced, and baseline primes. Reaction times are modeled with linear mixed effects over participants and items after accuracy/outlier exclusions; the reported outcome is condition-specific RT difference, including an 83.2 ms congruent-versus-baseline effect.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 2.1–2.2: participant count, four conditions, 96 trials, exclusions, and RT mixed-effects analysis.

records.eval: Using up to 1,000 held-out samples per speech, music, and sound domain, the study compares semantic and acoustic token distributions from HuBERT, EnCodec, and DAC. It evaluates rank-frequency/power-law behavior, N-gram language-model perplexity, normalized cross-entropy predictability, and TF-IDF/token-usage distributions; the domain and model are the comparison denominators.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.1–5.2: 960-hour training sources, held-out sample construction, tokenizers, PPL/TF-IDF objects, and domain comparisons.

records.eval: Synthetic corruption experiments fine-tune Robust-wav2vec2 with deletion, misspelling, sound-alike, repetition, and timestamp corruption at 25/50/75/100% mixed with clean transcripts, then fine-tune with 10 minutes of precise data. A real-world NCTE classroom case uses 5,235 hours, 17 gold classes/13 hours, and Wav2vec2 ASR; the paper compares recognition error across corruption and data configurations.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 2–3.2: TEDLIUM/NCTE corpus sizes, corruption rates, 150,000-step training, 10-minute precise fine-tuning, and classroom case-study design.

records.eval: Accent normalization is evaluated on seven accents from L2-ARCTIC/ARCTIC, with four speakers per accent, 50 validation and 80 held-out test sentences, and one unseen speaker per accent. WER, speaker-embedding cosine similarity, MUSHRA naturalness/accentedness, and best-worst speaker similarity are compared with a frame-to-frame baseline; subjective tests use 21 raters and 20 samples.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.1 and 4.4: accent/speaker splits, objective metrics, MUSHRA/BWS protocol, and held-out-speaker denominator.

records.eval: The multi-accent pronunciation frontend is tested on EDI and LDS1 accents against uni-accent baselines using word-boundary, prosodic-boundary, and word accuracy for seen and unseen tokens. The paper reports multi-accent accuracy near the uni-accent baseline, with seen-word scores above 99% and lower unseen-word accuracy as the harder transfer case.
records.evaluation_source: Section 4.1 and Table 3: EDI/LDS1 test accents, boundary/word metrics, seen-versus-unseen token split, and baseline comparison.

records.eval: The computational articulatory model generates 75 VCV syllables over five vowels and four consonant configurations, computes F1–F3 trajectories with a transmission-line model, and compares synthetic F2/F3 transition clusters with aggregated Öhman observations. The evaluation is geometric/formant trajectory agreement, not a listener or recognition study.
records.evaluation_source: Section 3: 75 synthetic VCV trajectories, Maeda parameters, transmission-line formants, and comparison with Öhman data.

records.eval: The study extracts 113,296 French oral vowels from eight hours of Corpus of Interactional Data, retains 112,346 after duration filtering, and identifies 6,373 in reduced sequences. Lobanov-normalized formants support pVSA, vowel-distinctiveness, and reduction-rate analyses across speakers and conversational contexts.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 2.1–2.3: corpus participants, vowel counts, duration filter, normalization, and acoustic metrics.

records.eval: Llama-SMoP is evaluated on 433 hours of LRS3 for ASR, VSR, and AVSR, with Llama-AVSR, DCI, and MM-Fuser baselines. WER is measured across model sizes and audio-noise SNR levels from 7.5 to −2.5 dB; the DEDR routing strategy is reported as the strongest SMoP variant.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.2 and Tables 1–2: LRS3 scope, tasks, baselines, WER metric, model configurations, and SNR conditions.

records.eval: Song-form-aware lyric generation is evaluated on approximately 340K training, 18K validation, and 10K evaluation samples from Genius Song Lyrics after toxicity filtering. Perplexity, syllable-count deviation, syllable-count error rate, and BERT-S similarity are compared across full, paragraph, line, phrase, and word generation levels against Front-P and related baselines.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.1–5: dataset split, toxicity filtering, PPL/SCD/SCErr/BERT-S metrics, granularity conditions, and baseline comparison.

records.eval: The codec experiments train on EARS-WHAM with 86.8 hours of training, 1.7 hours validation, and 3.7 hours test audio, using emotion/style variation and paired noisy-clean speech. Intrusive PESQ, STOI, ESTOI, and SI-SDR plus non-intrusive NISQA are evaluated, and Bjøntegaard-Delta rate compares bitrate at matched distortion across 16 and 48 kHz settings.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.2 and 4.2 Evaluation Metrics/Table 1: dataset partitions, objective metrics, sampling rates, and BD-rate comparison.

records.eval: The analysis uses 7,504 annotated stop tokens from Malaysian speakers across Malay, English, and Mandarin, with four dominance/repertoire groups. Closure voicing, VOT, burst intensity, vowel duration, and onset f0/F1 slopes are normalized by language and speaker and modeled with random-forest classification and cue-weight comparisons across languages and speaker groups.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 2.1–2.2: multilingual token counts, group design, acoustic annotation, normalization, and classification target.

records.eval: EmotionRankCLAP uses MSP-Podcast v1.12 with 90,022 training, 25,258 development, and 34,963 test utterances, each annotated by at least five raters for valence, arousal, and dominance. Cross-modal alignment is evaluated with MMD and Wasserstein distance against CLAP and contrastive baselines on 10-second, 16-kHz inputs.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.1 and Table 1: corpus splits, annotation aggregation, input preprocessing, baselines, and alignment metrics.

records.eval: DC-Spin is evaluated through zero-shot spoken-language-model tasks TSC, sWUGGY, and sBLIMP, plus speech resynthesis on Expresso dev/test utterances using original speaker/style IDs. It reports accuracy for the language tasks and ASR-WER, speaker similarity, and UTMOS for resynthesized speech, comparing against neural codec/tokenizer baselines.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.2: Expresso resynthesis split, task definitions, accuracy/WER/UTMOS objects, and baseline comparisons.

records.eval: DiceHuBERT compares HuBERT distillation methods on phoneme error rate, word error rate, unsupervised error rate, equal-error rate, and classification accuracy, with explicit upper and lower bounds. The paper notes that model/data choices and the 60k-hour pretraining scale limit direct comparison across the reported speech tasks.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4 and Tables 1–3: task metrics, baseline/upper/lower-bound construction, and reported comparison scope.

records.eval: Cross-speaker emotion transfer is evaluated with five-point naturalness, speaker-similarity, and emotion-similarity MOS, Whisper-Large WER/CER, WavLM speaker cosine similarity, and Emotion2Vec emotion similarity. Twenty participants rate two random samples per emotion for each evaluation speaker; objective measures use the full evaluation set.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.3–3.4: subjective protocol, objective metrics, participant count, and evaluation-set denominator.

records.eval: Temp4Cap is trained and evaluated on Clotho (5k 15–30-second clips) and AudioCaps (about 50k clips); validation/test clips have five reference captions. BLEU4, ROUGE-L, CIDEr, METEOR, SPIDEr, temporal accuracy, and temporal F1 are compared with CNN-encoder baselines, with MOS reported with 95% confidence intervals.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3–4 and Table 1: datasets, caption multiplicity, captioning metrics, temporal metrics, and baseline comparison.

records.eval: The diffusion TTS model is trained on approximately 585 hours of multi-speaker LibriTTS and evaluated on the 2.2-hour LibriSpeech-PC test-clean set. WER measures intelligibility and speaker similarity is measured against the F5-TTS Small baseline; the paper reports comparisons for the dual-modality alignment configuration.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.4: LibriTTS training corpus, LibriSpeech-PC test-clean scope, F5-TTS baseline, WER, and similarity metrics.

records.eval: Neural spectral-band generation is trained with about 70 hours of sound events, 30 hours of music, and 30 hours of speech, then evaluated on 43 USAC-standardization items: 11 speech, 18 music, and 14 mixed. NMR, 2f-model MMS, and ViSQOL MOS form the objective rate-distortion metrics; a 14-participant A/B test uses nine randomly selected clips.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.2–4.3 and Figures 3–4: training domains, 43-item test denominator, objective metrics, and listening-test protocol.

records.eval: The toolkit comparison uses speech from 77 participants with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders and 87 healthy controls performing picture-description tasks. OpenSMILE/eGeMAPS, Praat, and Librosa are run with standardized 16-kHz, 60-ms frame settings; feature agreement and extraction robustness are compared across clinical groups and acoustic feature types.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.3: participant counts, clinical/control groups, speech task, toolkits, and standardized extraction configuration.

records.eval: Tonal variation is analyzed on 4,294 high-falling-tone tokens from 16 Taiwan Southern Min speakers: 1,423 citation realizations and 2,871 sandhi realizations across 41 word types. F0 is sampled at 21 normalized time points and modeled with generalized additive models, with word meaning, tone type, speaker, and phonetic controls defining the comparison.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 2.1–2.2: speaker/token counts, F0 extraction grid, word-type filtering, and GAM analysis.

records.eval: The spatio-spectral diarization pipeline is evaluated on 10-minute LibriCSS eight-speaker meetings with 0–40% overlap and LibriW ASN re-recordings in two rooms with T60 values of 200/800 ms. Four microphones are used for diarization and DER is reported without a forgiveness collar; downstream seven-channel ASR uses concatenated minimum-permutation WER via MeetEval.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.3: datasets, rooms/overlap, microphone configurations, DER/cpWER definitions, and comparison systems.

records.eval: MSDA is evaluated for six source-to-target Greek domain transfers using target-domain WER, comparing supervised source fine-tuning, continual pretraining, M2DS2, Meta pseudo-labeling, CASTLE, and MSDA. The corpora include 72-hour Logotypografia, 12-hour Common Voice, 99-hour HParl, and weakly supervised Greek Podcast subsets, with greedy decoding in the reported table.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.2–3.3 and Table 1: domain sizes, six transfer directions, WER metric, decoding condition, and baselines.

records.eval: The analyze-then-enhance system is evaluated on mixed speech with variable speaker counts using separation, denoising, and dereverberation metrics against its analyzer/enhancer baselines. The controlled tests vary the number of speakers and acoustic degradation; the paper reports the measured signal-recovery and perceptual-quality outcomes within those mixture conditions.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3–4: analyzer/enhancer construction, variable-speaker mixture conditions, and reported comparison protocol.

records.eval: Conditional flow matching for dysarthric-speech reconstruction is tested on seen and unseen speakers, comparing discrete-unit and mel-spectrogram inputs against wav2vec2-base-960h and a dataset-finetuned wav2vec2 baseline. WER measures transcription intelligibility and 23 self-reported English listeners rate 10 random test utterances on a 1–5 MOS scale; seen/unseen speaker results are separated.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4–5 and Tables 1–2: Speech Accessibility Project test subset, baselines, WER/MOS definitions, listener count, and seen/unseen split.

records.eval: NeuroSpex+ uses 128 KULeuven speech-EEG trials from 16 subjects in subject-independent 16-fold cross-validation, with 4-second windows yielding 39,984 training and 2,856 validation/test segments per fold. Speaker extraction is evaluated with SDRi, SI-SDRi, PESQ, and STOI; envelope reconstruction uses Pearson correlation, compared with NeuroSpex, NeuroHeed, and BISS.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.3: subject/fold design, segment counts, metrics, and baselines.

records.eval: Voxplorer is evaluated as an interactive voice-data exploration dashboard: feature extraction, dimensionality reduction, filtering, and projection are tested on the paper's voice datasets through the supported visual-analysis workflow. The evidence concerns exploratory usability and inspectable projections rather than a held-out recognition metric or listener denominator.
records.evaluation_source: Captured paper method/results sections describing the dashboard workflow, feature projections, and interactive exploration boundary.

records.eval: Depression detection uses 698 D-Vlog waveforms from 961 annotated vlogs, split by unique YouTube account into stratified train/development sets (294/261 train and 73/69 development depression/normal instances). Speech-level and segment-level AST models are compared with AUC on the development set, with 5,000 bootstrap samples for 95% intervals and DeLong's test; no independent test set is used.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.4 and Table 2: corpus attrition, account-level split, class counts, AUC/CI procedure, comparison, and missing independent test boundary.

records.eval: The Transcription Portal workflow is demonstrated on four 1976 Italian oral-history interviews with five Ravensbrück survivors and approximately 18 hours of speech digitized at 96 kHz/24-bit. Evaluation is a bounded transcription-workflow demonstration comparing ASR-generated SRT material with manual correction and export, not a held-out WER experiment; corpus access and editor operations are the evidence objects.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 2.1–3: four interviews/five speakers, 18-hour archive, digitization details, ASR preview, manual correction, and export workflow.

records.eval: Tonal contrasts are measured from 1,152 recordings by eight Malipo speakers (four male, four female) across test words and repetitions. Tone-bearing-unit F0 contours are Log-Z normalized and duration is measured; linear mixed-effects models use tonal and vowel types as fixed effects and speakers as random effects to compare lexical tone categories.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 2.1–3: speaker/sample counts, acoustic measures, normalization, mixed-effects structure, and tonal comparison.

records.eval: SiamCTC is evaluated on LibriSpeech train-clean-100 with HuBERT and WavLM encoders and compared with Spin and LASER variants under SUPERB conditions. Phoneme Error Rate and Word Error Rate are reported on LibriSpeech test-clean, with additional speed-perturbed evaluation and ablations of the monotonic-alignment loss.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.1–4.4 and Table 1: corpus splits, encoder/baseline set, PER/WER metrics, test-clean denominator, and robustness condition.

records.eval: Parkinson's-speech analysis uses 80 speakers, 40 with Parkinson's disease and 40 healthy controls, reading and retelling a text. Five-fold external nested cross-validation evaluates frame-wise and subject-wise classification with accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F1; lexical/linguistic analyses use only held-out test predictions to avoid leakage.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 2.1 and 3: matched PD/HC cohort, tasks, nested folds, baseline, metrics, and held-out prediction boundary.

records.eval: MMLoRA is evaluated on IEMOCAP's 5,531 utterances across four emotion classes using leave-one-session-out cross-validation. Weighted accuracy and unweighted accuracy compare zero-shot, few-shot, vanilla-LoRA, and MMLoRA configurations under the same Video-LLaMA audio branch and routing settings.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.4: dataset/class count, cross-validation, baselines, prompt conditions, WA/UA metrics, and reported ablation.

records.eval: The spectrogram-inversion methods are trained on LibriSpeech train-clean-360 (363.6 hours, 921 speakers) and evaluated on 50 random utterances from test-clean (5.4 hours, 40 speakers). ESTOI, SI-SDR, and PESQ compare the proposed neural/numerical methods across window sizes from 128 to 8192, with runtime also reported.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.2–4.3: train/test speaker-hour counts, random test sample, objective metrics, window-size sweep, and runtime comparison.

records.eval: Dialect classification uses 10-second segments with speaker-disjoint train/validation/test partitions; each validation/test split samples speakers by dialect and the experiment repeats 250 random subsets. Retrieval-based voice conversion is compared with frequency masking and segment-removal augmentation using mean weighted F1, with Mann–Whitney U tests for run comparisons.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.2: segment length, speaker-disjoint partition, 250-run protocol, augmentation baselines, metric, and significance test.

records.eval: The AAC/TTS system is evaluated through its speech-access workflow on the captured participant/task materials, comparing static versus dynamic communication support and zero-shot TTS outputs. The reported evidence is task- and user-facing generation behavior rather than a conventional held-out recognition benchmark; accessibility and output quality are bounded by the demonstrated scenario.
records.evaluation_source: Captured paper experiment and evaluation sections describing AAC task materials, dynamic imagery, and zero-shot TTS comparison.

records.eval: AuralNet is tested on synthetic binaural TIMIT convolved with ITA HRTFs, with 98,136 training samples, 2,088 single-source validation samples, and 2,800 multi-source test samples across seen and unseen rooms, speech, source counts, and 20/10/0-dB SNR. Detection accuracy, F1, and detection-aware angular error measure source-sector detection and azimuth/elevation error; comparisons are reported for one-, two-, and three-talker cases.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.2 and Table 1: HRTF/noise construction, split counts, seen/unseen-room protocol, source/SNR conditions, and three evaluation metrics.

records.eval: Neurodyne is evaluated for global-key and template-based pitch manipulation against WORLD, TD-PSOLA, DiffPitcher, SiFi-GAN, PC-NSF, and ground truth. Global-key tests report F0RMSE plus quality and similarity MUSHRA ratings for shifts from -12 to +12 semitones; variance and transient manipulations are also tested over musical-note and transient-duration conditions. The paper gives MUSHRA confidence intervals but does not make the listener/sample denominator prominent in the extracted section.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1 and Tables 1–2: manipulation settings, baseline systems, F0RMSE/MUSHRA objects, pitch-shift range, and reported confidence intervals.

records.eval: VNSC is evaluated on the TaL80 corpus: 11,478 training, 810 validation, and 1,140 mutually exclusive test utterances from 81 speakers, at a 6-kbps codec rate. PESQ, CSIG, CBAK, COVL, STOI, and ViSQOL compare visual-available and visual-unavailable VNSC with MDCTCodec, SoundStream, Encodec, and HiFi-Codec; a validation ablation varies feature-fusion depth and image reconstruction loss, and a noisy test set adds SSNR.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–4.3 and Tables 1–3: TaL80 split, codec/test conditions, objective metrics, baselines, fusion/loss ablations, and noise-robustness protocol.

records.eval: The adaptive IIR hear-through filter is evaluated in 16-kHz simulations against FxBLMS/F, equation-error adaptive IIR, delayless sub-band FIR, and fixed-filter baselines. Single-source tests use multi-tone, bandlimited-noise, and broadband-noise stimuli; dynamic indoor/outdoor simulations vary moving and multiple source directions. Steady-state MSE and convergence behavior are the reported outcomes, with the proposed filter reaching -50 dB or lower SS-MSE in the three single-source tests.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.2 and Figure 3: sampling rate, signal constructions, baseline set, dynamic-scene conditions, SS-MSE outcome, and convergence comparison.

records.eval: Low-resource ASR is evaluated on held-out parallel-corpus test sentences for six Middle Eastern languages, with remaining recordings used for training and validation merged into training. Untuned Whisper Base/Small zero-shot baselines are compared with multilingual and monolingual fine-tuning using WER and CER; results include 1,000-bootstrap significance tests (200 for Zazaki), with monolingual mean WER 64.4 versus multilingual 60.5 and language-specific outcomes reported by language.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.1–5.1 and Table 2: test-set construction, Whisper configurations, WER/CER definitions, language-level results, and bootstrap significance procedure.

records.eval: Gaze-enhanced turn-taking prediction is tested on manually labeled portions of the 30-hour RLR-CHAT triadic-conversation corpus. Six sessions provide pretraining and four manually labeled sessions are split 60/20/20 for train/validation/test; target-VAD, single-user gaze, and multi-user gaze models are compared. Macro-F1 is reported for role classes and behavior classes, with additional transition-level (one-second post-transition) and group-level event analyses.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3 and 5.1–5.3 plus Tables 1–2: RLR-CHAT scope, session split, baselines, macro-F1, and transition/group evaluation definitions.

records.eval: The articulatory/acoustic comparison uses 590 tokens from 97 French disyllabic target words produced by three women with Moebius syndrome and three controls. Forced-aligned duration, F1–F3 at vowel midpoint, and tongue/lip sensor x/y/z positions are compared between accented and unaccented vowels using Bayesian regressions with vowel, state, interaction, and by-speaker intercepts. Four chains of 4,000 iterations and 95% HDIs with a standardized [-0.1,0.1] ROPE define clear differences versus tendencies.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 2.1–2.3 and 3: participant/token counts, acoustic/articulatory measures, Bayesian model structure, sampling settings, and HDI/ROPE decision rule.

records.eval: UTP is evaluated on BVCC speech-quality assessment and IEMOCAP continuous speech-emotion recognition. BVCC contains 4,973 train, 1,066 development, and 1,066 test utterances with listener scores; IEMOCAP contains 10,039 utterances and 5-fold session-held-out validation. SRCC and LCC measure system-level SQA and utterance-level CSER, with 20 SQA runs and averaged cross-validation results comparing UTMOS/UTP, mean-listener scales, listener embeddings, and comparison scores.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.1–4.4 and Tables 1–2: BVCC/IEMOCAP denominators, listener-score construction, split protocol, SRCC/LCC metrics, run count, cross-validation, and comparison conditions.

records.eval: LombardTokenizer is evaluated on LibriSpeech, AVID, and FLombard, with 24 utterances from eight speakers at four vocal-effort levels in each effort-conversion test; conversion yields 27,648 evaluated sentences per AVID/FLombard dataset. PESQ/STOI assess synthesis quality, WER content preservation, EER speaker similarity, and JS-F0/JS-Slope acoustic consistency. A perceptual test uses 40 native listeners per dataset and 192 comparative ratings per dataset under intra- and inter-speaker conditions.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.2 and Tables 1–2: dataset/sample construction, objective metrics, listener protocol, baselines, and reported confidence/significance boundaries.

records.eval: TES-VC is evaluated on 200 GPT-4o-generated speaker descriptions paired with AudioCaps environmental descriptions and LibriTTS-R test-clean source speech. Fifteen listeners rate speaker consistency, environmental faithfulness, and realness on five-point MOS scales; age/gender recognition accuracy is also reported. Separate objective tests use 200 LibriTTS-R-Test samples with eight unseen reference speakers for WER/CER, and an AC-filter test set for CLAP and KL divergence, comparing VoiceLDM and FreeVC plus a no-adapter ablation.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.3 and Tables 1–2: prompt/test construction, listener count and MOS criteria, unseen-speaker objective set, metrics, baselines, and ablation.

records.eval: DOA-guided speech extraction is evaluated on synthetic six-speaker, noisy, reverberant 4-second mixtures generated from LibriSpeech and DEMAND, with 14.4k/3.6k/2k train/validation/test mixtures. SDRi, SI-SDRi, and PESQ measure extraction quality while parameter count measures efficiency; ablations vary one-hot versus cyclic DOA embeddings, beamwidth, and inactive DOA inputs, and comparisons include MVDR and JNF. A downstream two-dataset ASR test reports WER.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–4.1 and Tables 1–2: mixture construction, split counts, metrics, DOA/beam ablations, baselines, and downstream WER evaluation.

records.eval: LinearVC is evaluated on LibriSpeech test-clean with 7,800 conversions per model, using WER/CER for intelligibility and speaker-verification EER for speaker similarity. MUSHRA-like tests evaluate naturalness and similarity with roughly five-second utterances, ten target speakers, at least 15 raters per conversion, real/degraded anchors, 95% confidence intervals, and Friedman/Wilcoxon tests. A LibriSpeech dev-clean experiment varies factorization transformations and rank to expose the intelligibility–speaker-similarity tradeoff.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.2 and Tables 1–2: conversion denominator, objective/subjective metrics, listener/anchor protocol, significance tests, and dev-clean rank sweep.

records.eval: Vocoder-Projected Feature Discriminator is evaluated on VCTK and LibriTTS using UTMOS, DNSMOS, Whisper-large-v3 CER, Resemblyzer SECS, training time, and peak memory. Ablations vary discriminator upsampling depth, pretraining/freezing, and alternative acceleration strategies; the main subjective comparison uses 90 speaker/sentence pairs, ground-truth and DiffVC-30 anchors, and more than 1,000 responses from 11 participants for five-point quality MOS and four-point similarity MOS.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.3 and Tables 1–5: corpora, objective metrics, compute measures, ablation axes, subjective denominator, listener count, anchors, and confidence intervals.

records.eval: Spotlight-TTS is tested on the 17,500-sample Emotional Speech Dataset: ten English speakers, 350 sentences, and five emotions. Naturalness and similarity use 50 test samples (five per speaker) rated by 20 participants with 95% intervals; objective evaluation over the full test set uses UTMOS, Whisper WER, WavLM SECS, F0 and periodicity RMSE, and voiced/unvoiced F1. FastSpeech2-GST/CSE, StyleSpeech, GenerSpeech, and loss/architecture ablations provide comparisons.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.3 and Tables 1–4: ESD composition, subjective sample/listener protocol, objective metrics, baseline models, and ablation conditions.

records.eval: Diversity/independence regularization is evaluated primarily with CTC, AED, and RNN-T models on LibriSpeech test-clean/test-other, measuring WER and relative error-rate reduction under Viterbi, beam, and greedy decoding without language models. CTC robustness tests use TEDLIUM2 dev/test, CHiME-3 dt/et, and KsponSpeech eval-clean/eval-other; OOD comparisons and ablations are run on CHiME-3 and TEDLIUM2. Checkpoints are selected by validation WER.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.1–4.2 and Tables 1–5: corpus/split scope, architectures, decoding conditions, WER/RERR metrics, OOD/robustness sets, and ablations.

records.eval: Child-wearable voice-type classification is evaluated with F-score, identification error rate, and percentage correct using a held-out set under the DARCLE annotation scheme. PyanNet-VTC and Whisper-VTC with frozen Whisper tiny/base/small representations are compared across child, other-child, male-adult, and female-adult classes, with a second human annotator as a performance ceiling. The best Whisper-small mean F-score is 53.6% versus 69.8% for human 2, with OCH remaining the hardest class.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 2.2–3.4 and Table 2: dataset augmentation/hold-out boundary, metrics, model variants, class-wise results, and human comparison.

records.eval: Diffusion Buffer is evaluated on the 54-hour EARS-WHAM speech-enhancement corpus, whose noisy mixtures span 0–15 dB SNR. PESQ and reference-free WVMOS are reported, with ESTOI used in the intelligibility comparison; tests vary buffer size and reverse diffusion steps and compare vanilla score-based enhancement, OUVE, BBED, and DEMUCS. WVMOS values clipped below 1.0 are a stated metric-handling boundary.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.3–5 and Figures 1–2: EARS-WHAM scope, SNR range, metrics, baselines, buffer/reverse-step sweeps, and WVMOS clipping rule.

records.eval: WhisperM2M is evaluated for many-to-many speech translation across six languages using CoVoST2 and Fleurs test sets. Case-sensitive sacreBLEU is averaged over specified X-EN, EN-X, and X-X language directions, comparing Whisper small/medium, SeamlessM4T medium, and SeamlessM4T large v2; decoder efficiency uses average latency per token on 1,000 CoVoST2 utterances over 10 runs on one H800. Training uses approximately 100k hours with cloud-generated pseudo-translation labels.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.4 and Table 1: language/data scope, BLEU aggregation, baselines, latency denominator/repeats, and pseudo-label provenance.

records.eval: Counterfactual Activation Editing is evaluated with Tacotron 2 trained on LJSpeech (12,500/500/100 train/validation/test clips). Prosody control compares direct, manifold-preserving, prototype-constrained, and truncation edits using Whisper PER; pronunciation correction uses 78 held-out target-word samples and WER, PER, sentence-embedding cosine similarity, and token similarity. A 20-listener CMOS test compares corrected with initial speech.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.2 and 5.2–5.3 plus Tables 1–2: LJSpeech split, edit variants, 78-sample correction set, objective metrics, listener count, and CMOS protocol.

records.eval: The streaming TTS acoustic model is evaluated on 500 test utterances from seen speakers, with objective metrics computed over all 500 and subjective listening on the selected test material. CER, SECS, UTMOS, real-time factor, latency, MOS, and similarity MOS compare the proposed Mamba/RVQ variants with streaming baselines; MOS/SMOS use five-point ratings and 95% confidence intervals, while ablations remove masked-language-model and INR components.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.1–4.6 and Table 1: 500-utterance test denominator, objective/subjective metrics, baseline/ablation scope, and confidence-interval reporting.

records.eval: LRBA is evaluated on Google Speech Commands v2 using GSCv2-10 and GSCv2-30, split 90/5/5 into train/validation/test. Attack effectiveness uses accuracy variance and trigger attack success rate on the test set; stealthiness uses five-point MOS and the number of poisoned samples, with ResNet-34 and other speech-classification victims compared against backdoor baselines. The paper reports model-agnostic and trigger/poison-count variants.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.1–4.2 and Table 3: GSCv2 task variants/splits, AV/ASR/PN/MOS definitions, victim models, and baseline comparison.

records.eval: Long-context speech synthesis is evaluated on 20 sentence-level samples and 10 roughly 60-second long-form samples, rated by 10 native Mandarin listeners on MOS and CoMOS scales from 1 to 5 with 95% intervals. Objective measures are speaker-vector similarity, CER from Paraformer-zh, and SpeechBERTScore; experiments compare MMCE-Qformer, CLAP-RAG, the proposed memory/prefix-mask model, and module ablations while reporting context-token cost.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.3 and Table 1: audiobook training corpus, subjective sample/listener denominators, objective metrics, baselines, ablations, and context-cost measures.

records.eval: EME-TTS is evaluated for emphasis and emotion on the established EmoSpeech ESD splits, with test/validation utterance counts specified by the source split. Objective tests report emphasis recognition and emotion accuracy over 1,550 synthesized samples per model; subjective tasks use 11 listeners, including 80 shuffled emotion-identification samples, ranking sets, and 100 balanced-emotion MOS samples. NISQA and MOS, plus comparisons with EmoSpeech and CosyVoice2, assess output quality and expressiveness.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.2 and Tables 1–4: split provenance, objective sample denominator, listener count/tasks, metrics, baselines, and balanced MOS protocol.

records.eval: Synthetic dysarthric speech is tested for ASR augmentation using speaker-partitioned authentic and synthetic data in an 8:1:1 train/validation/test split, with two synthetic sets generated per speaker and seven training-set combinations. CER measures dysarthric-speech recognition; acoustic similarity uses F0/duration statistics, RM-C, MFCC cosine similarity, PESQ, and average speaker similarity, with means and t-tests comparing synthetic with authentic speech. The paper explicitly treats synthetic data as supplementary rather than a substitute.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4–5 and Tables 1–3: split/design, synthetic-data combinations, CER and acoustic metrics, statistical testing, and authenticity limitation.

records.eval: SA-RAS is evaluated on speaker-disjoint LibriTTS splits with validation speakers 10 and test speakers 12, while ESD's 10 English and 10 Chinese speakers/350 parallel utterances are used to inspect retrieval-space behavior. Objective evaluation reports DTW-aligned MCD, energy error, F0 error, and emotion cosine similarity; 15 native listeners rate 15 samples from three unseen speakers on naturalness, style similarity, and style-text compatibility MOS with 95% intervals. Retrieval baselines include paired, CA-CLAP, random, and no-speaker ablations.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.5 and Table 1: speaker-disjoint splits, ESD retrieval set, objective/subjective metrics, listener/sample denominator, baselines, and ablation.

records.eval: Foldable Conformer and wav2vec2 compression are evaluated on NIST Hub5'00, RT02, RT03, and LibriSpeech test-clean, with WER as the principal accuracy measure and MAPSSWE at alpha 0.05 for significance. Experiments vary executed depth, layer folding, joint training, self-distillation, and comparison compression methods; averaged WER across the three conversational evaluation sets is reported for Conformer systems, while test-clean is reported for wav2vec2 systems.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.1–4.4 and Tables 1–4: evaluation corpora, WER aggregation, significance test, depth/folding axes, ablations, and comparison scope.

records.eval: Cantonese tone-merger analysis uses perceptually selected correct and merged productions from participants, with eight additional participants chosen to balance merger groups. Average pitch, slope, and curvature features for three tone pairs feed Random Forest models separately for competitive and non-competitive lexical contexts; five-fold cross-validation selects tree counts and outputs are checked against perceptual labels and contour divergence. Production accuracy and mixed-effects/GCA models test competition, age, gender, and tone-pair effects, with an 80% threshold defining merger.
records.evaluation_source: Methods and Sections 3.1–3.2: participant selection, acoustic features, cross-validation, perceptual-label comparison, accuracy outcome, grouping threshold, and statistical model.

records.eval: SpeechSEC is evaluated on LibriTTS-R train-clean subsets with test-clean held out, across speech synthesis, editing, and continuation using SpeechTokenizer, SpeechTokenizer/DAC, and HuBERT/DAC token configurations. WER/CER measure intelligibility, MOS-style audio quality and cosine similarity measure quality/voice preservation, and RTX 3090 acoustic-token generation time measures efficiency; continuation omits WER/CER because generated content is variable. Baselines and edit/continuation ablations isolate the multi-task benefit.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.2 and Tables 1–3: LibriTTS-R split, task/configuration scope, metrics, hardware timing, inapplicable continuation metrics, baselines, and ablations.

records.eval: NR-LauraTTS is evaluated first as a speech-enhancement codec denoiser against CMGAN and MP-SENet using DNSMOS P.835 SIG, BAK, and OVRL plus FLOPs, then as noise-robust zero-shot TTS on 3–10-second test samples with same-speaker noisy prompts. SECS, Whisper-large-v3 WER/CER, MOS, and SMOS are reported; more than 30 Mechanical Turk raters each score 20 samples on 1–5 scales with 95% MOS/SMOS intervals. Clean-prompt, noisy-prompt, MP-SENet, and NR-LauraTTS conditions bound the comparison.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.2–4.2 and Tables 1–3: enhancement/TTS tasks, prompt/test construction, metrics, rater protocol, confidence intervals, baselines, and compute comparison.

records.eval: The unified audio-visual multi-talker model is evaluated on speaker-disjoint LRS3 splits with noisy overlapped speech and visual speaker tags. WER measures transcription, while visual WER (VWER) measures whether the correct face is associated with the words and visual time error rate (VTER) measures temporal speaker attribution; tag/no-tag, single-/multi-talker, and model-component conditions are compared. Validation-based early stopping and the longer held-out test utterances define the reported boundary.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.1–4.4 and Table 1: LRS3 speaker-disjoint construction, overlap/noise conditions, WER/VWER/VTER definitions, ablations, and test-set caveat.

records.eval: staRt is evaluated as an accessible visual-acoustic biofeedback application for /r/ speech training rather than through a held-out recognition benchmark. The reported evidence is the real-time LPC-spectrum implementation, target-formant slider, clinician scoring/adaptive exercises, iOS/web deployment, and WebRTC telepractice workflow. Peak-picking and formant tracking are explicitly not yet stable enough for automated correctness feedback, so clinical efficacy and generalization remain open evaluation questions.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3–4: LPC processing parameters, user-facing task features, deployment/telepractice demonstration, and explicit future-work limitation on automated evaluation.

records.eval: TagThunder is presented as an experimental framework and browser add-on for concurrent spatialized speech tag clouds and skimming/scanning strategies. Evaluation evidence is the implemented processing pipeline—web-zone segmentation, YAKE keyword extraction, Kokoro synthesis, Web Audio 3D spatialization, and four navigation strategies—plus the downloadable add-on. The paper explicitly states that the framework lacks full accessibility features for end users and reports no participant study, task accuracy, latency benchmark, or listener denominator.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 2–3 and artifact note: implemented pipeline, strategy definitions, downloadable artifact, and explicit absence of end-user evaluation.

records.eval: Eigenvoice speaker generation is evaluated on VCTK using 10 base speakers (five male, five female), 100 generated speakers, and 10 test sentences per generated speaker. MOS and WER compare the proposed model with an x-vector-based method; speaker diversity is measured from Resemblyzer embeddings using t-SNE and maximum cosine similarity to the 10 ground-truth base speakers, with generated-speaker similarity spanning approximately 0.82–0.97. The evaluation prioritizes diversity over absolute synthesis quality.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.2–4.3 and Figures 2–3: VCTK/base-speaker construction, MOS/WER comparison, embedding protocol, diversity statistic, and stated objective boundary.

records.eval: Multimodal L2-English scoring is evaluated on 29,857 Korean-learner speech samples split into 20,965 train, 4,501 validation, and 4,391 test samples. Two expert raters provide 1–5 scores for task completion, delivery, accuracy, and appropriateness; models are compared with unimodal, integrated multimodal, and independent multimodal baselines using Pearson correlation coefficient for each score and the final level. The best wav2vec2+BERT model reports average PCC 0.734 with SD 0.0129, using an in-house ASR transcript stream with 14.2% WER.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–4.1 and Tables 1–2: dataset splits, expert-rating targets, transcript provenance, PCC/SD metrics, and baseline comparison.

records.eval: The portable multiple-sound-spot system is evaluated as a Show & Tell demonstration rather than a held-out acoustic or translation benchmark. The demonstrated configurations are eight-language synthesis, eight simultaneous English-content zones, and four-language synthesis combined with Japanese-to-English/Chinese/Korean simultaneous speech-to-speech translation, running on a backpack-carried 16-loudspeaker array, on-premise laptop, wireless microphone, and compact amplifier. The paper reports implementation dimensions and portability but no participant, localization-error, latency, intelligibility, or translation-accuracy denominator.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3–4 and Figure 3: hardware/system configuration, three demonstration scenarios, and explicit demonstration-only evidence boundary.

records.eval: Bilingual visually grounded speech models are evaluated with familiar and mutual-exclusivity (ME) two-image discrimination tests on speaker-disjoint test samples. Each class contributes 50 episodes per test, experiments repeat across five training seeds, and monolingual/bilingual English, French, and Dutch models are compared. Familiar accuracy validates learning, while ME accuracy above 50% quantifies the bias: monolingual models are about 67–68%, with bilingual English/French or English/Dutch training reducing English ME accuracy to 65.7% or 63.5%.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 2.4–3.1 and Table 1: test protocol, episode/seed denominators, language conditions, familiar/ME definitions, and reported accuracy/standard errors.

records.eval: TS-URGENet is evaluated on an official validation set and an official blind test set using DNSMOS, NISQA, UTMOS, PESQ/POLQA, ESTOI, SDR, MCD, LSD, SpeechBERTScore, phonetic similarity, speaker similarity, content accuracy, and MOS. Ablations add metric-aware fine-tuning terms and joint-stage training; the blind test compares the final model with a baseline across the full metric panel. The official blind-set origin and metric-specific tradeoffs bound the claim beyond the reported benchmark.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.1–4.2 and Tables 3–4: official validation/blind-set conditions, metric panel, ablation sequence, baseline comparison, and tradeoff discussion.

records.eval: Tungnaá is evaluated as an interactive artistic text-to-voice performance system using its IATV dataset, reduced phonetic alphabet representation, and live performance workflow. Evidence concerns the implementation's real-time worker/GUI architecture, customizability on small bespoke datasets, latent feedback control, and performance deployment; the paper does not provide a held-out recognition score, listener study, latency table, or conventional quantitative denominator.
records.evaluation_source: System description and IATV/Tungnaá sections: dataset/workflow, interactive controls, deployment evidence, and absence of conventional benchmark evaluation.

records.eval: Near-end listening enhancement is evaluated in simulations using speech from Dantale II, American English, AEMST, and TIMIT, competing-speaker noise, speech-shaped noise, and UrbanSound8K backgrounds across SNR conditions. OptFractASII and competing spectral-shaping/time-frequency allocation methods are compared with ESTOI, STGI, and related intelligibility/quality measures; results are pooled over speech datasets and grouped SNR ranges. The evidence is simulation-based and does not establish listener-level or real-device performance.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.3 and Figures 1–4: speech/noise corpora, SNR/mixture conditions, objective metric comparisons, pooling, and simulation boundary.

records.eval: SpecTokenizer is evaluated as a compressed-spectrum neural codec at 6, 4, and 0.5 kbps, with ASR WER, PESQ, STOI, SDR, Mel-spectrum loss, UTMOS, and XLSR-MOS as reported objective measures. Comparisons cover other codec models; ablations vary spectrum design, codebook size, frame rate, bitrate, and model miniaturization, with parameter/compute cost also reported. The evaluation establishes rate-distortion and intelligibility comparisons under the paper's test protocol, not broad perceptual or deployment reliability.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.4–4.5 and Tables 2–5: bitrate conditions, metric panel, codec baselines, ablations, miniaturization, and compute comparison.

records.eval: FlowSE is evaluated on the DNS Challenge Interspeech 2021 test set under reverberant, non-reverberant, and real-recording conditions, plus a simulated VCTK/noise test set with unseen mixtures. DNSMOS is the primary speech-quality measure on the challenge set; the simulated set reports WER and real-time factor, with comparisons to diffusion and non-diffusion enhancement systems. The paper explicitly notes that standard PESQ/SI-SNR may not reflect perceptual quality and uses neural MOS accordingly.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.1–4.4 and Tables 1–2: public/constructed test sets, acoustic conditions, DNSMOS/WER/RTF metrics, baselines, and metric limitation.

records.eval: Individualized speech enhancement is evaluated using simulated hearing profiles and a one-hour DNS-Challenge-derived test set at 0-dB SNR and 70-dB SPL. HASPI and HASQI assess intelligibility and quality for hearing-aided listeners; NRMSE and SRMR assess cochlear-synaptopathy-related enhancement behavior. Noise training uses AudioSet and Freesound test noise, while the paper reports no listener validation yet and identifies a future listening test.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1 and 4 plus Tables 2–4: hearing-profile simulation, one-hour test denominator, SNR/SPL condition, objective metrics, noise provenance, and missing listening-study boundary.

records.eval: Prenuclear-glide organization in Hefei Mandarin is analyzed from recordings by 10 local college students, with three excluded and seven participants retained. Annotated acoustic time points and formants define stability, duration, and centering measures for jV/CjV, wV/CwV, and related syllable pairs; linear mixed-effects models with participant effects test RSD and duration differences. The evidence is a small controlled production sample, not a recognition or perceptual generalization benchmark.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 2.1–3 and Tables 1–5: participant inclusion/exclusion, acoustic annotations, measured intervals/formants, mixed-effects comparisons, and sample-size boundary.

records.eval: Zero-shot accent robustness is evaluated with CER on L2-ARCTIC English, MAGICDATA Mandarin, and CommonVoice Spanish, varying speaker count, per-speaker duration, accent diversity, and single-speaker training. Test scope includes 24 non-native English speakers/six accents, 43 Mandarin speakers/28.1 hours, 647 Spanish speakers/2.3 hours, and an approximately 3.2-hour English test subset; topline models are trained with test accents in-distribution, while single-speaker tests use L1-ARCTIC and FLEURS. CER is used because it correlates strongly with WER in the reported evaluation.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.2 and Tables 1–2/Figures 1–4: language datasets, speaker/hour denominators, accent/topline construction, CER metric, and in-/out-of-distribution boundary.

records.eval: Changde Mandarin tone perception is tested in two experiments with 30 participants: Experiment 1 presents 240 randomized [mi] stimuli across four tones and five pitch-register levels, recording identification and reaction time; Experiment 2 has 15 participants in AX and 15 in ABX discrimination tasks over tone continua with repeated randomized stimuli. Identification and discrimination accuracy are modeled against pitch register, slope, and continuum, with post-hoc comparisons distinguishing categorical and gradient perception.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 2.2–3.2 and Figures 1–7: stimulus count, participant/task allocation, randomization/repetition, response measures, and perceptual analysis.

records.eval: Ordinal-Dep is evaluated on the DAIC-WOZ depression corpus of 189 interview participants, using the development subset as validation and the held-out test subset for reporting. Utterances are segmented into 3.84-second chunks, subject decisions use majority votes over segments, and macro-F1, positive-class F1, and negative-class F1 compare the proposed ordinal model with state-of-the-art and regression/classification ablations. Each experiment is repeated five times and averaged; PHQ-8 score >=10 defines depression.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4.1–4.4 and Tables 1–3: DAIC-WOZ cohort/split, chunking, PHQ-8 threshold, subject-level aggregation, metrics, repetitions, baselines, and ablations.

records.eval: VoxAging contains 293 speakers with longitudinal English/Mandarin recordings spanning up to about 17 years. Speaker-aging experiments compare ECAPA and ERes2Net verification systems using EER on held-out speaker-recognition conditions and embedding cosine similarity across recordings, with analyses stratified by age group and gender. The evidence measures temporal verification drift in a dataset resource; it does not isolate biological aging from channel, language, or recording-history effects.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3–4 and Tables 2–4: VoxAging composition, verification setup, EER/cosine metrics, model comparisons, and age/gender analyses.

records.eval: Patient-aware lung-sound classification is evaluated on the 6,898-recording ICBHI 2017 corpus using its official 60/40 train/test split. Five-run comparisons report sensitivity, specificity, and ICBHI score for normal/abnormal and four-class tasks, with pretrained-backbone, cohesion-separation, and global-alignment ablations. The benchmark is clinical-audio classification evidence, not validation of a deployed diagnostic system.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–3.4 and Tables 1–3: ICBHI size/split, repeated runs, clinical metrics, task settings, backbone/loss ablations, and deployment boundary.

records.eval: This paper evaluates subjective speech-synthesis research methodology rather than a new synthesizer: its evidence is a checklist and reproducibility-report recipe covering hypothesis, dataset bias, participant cohort, stimuli, protocol, analysis, conclusions, and limitations. The proposed evaluation object is whether another researcher can reconstruct the listening experiment; no new MOS denominator or model benchmark is claimed.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4–5: evaluation-campaign checklist, participant/material/reporting requirements, reproducibility recipe, and explicit methodological scope.

records.eval: FoleyMaster is evaluated on VGGSound Plus with CLIP Score for semantic alignment and onset detection accuracy for temporal alignment, compared with video-to-audio baselines. A 20-participant pairwise user study evaluates anonymized generated samples, while prompt-learning and probabilistic-time ablations isolate the proposed components. Automatic metrics and the small unfamiliar-listener study are proxies for video-grounded Foley usefulness.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3.1–4 and Tables 2–6: VGGSound Plus evaluation, semantic/temporal metrics, 20-participant study, baselines, and ablations.

records.eval: CLAP-ART is evaluated on AudioCaps and a second audio-caption benchmark with BLEU, METEOR, ROUGE-L, CIDEr, SPICE, and SPIDEr. Results include six-run averages, codebook and BEATs representation ablations, and comparisons with systems trained with or without extra audio-text data. Caption metrics measure reference agreement and only indirectly establish event-level grounding.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 4–5 and Tables 1–4: benchmark scope, caption metrics, repeated runs, codebook ablations, extra-data boundary, and SOTA comparisons.

records.eval: Direct-path relative harmonic detection is tested in simulated reverberant scenes varying source number and T60 and in recorded experimental conditions. Mean absolute angular error compares the proposal with four baselines, while valid direct-path-bin proportion diagnoses the spatial evidence available to localization. Results are bounded by the array geometry, harmonic assumptions, and simulated/recorded room protocol.
records.evaluation_source: Section 4 and Tables 1–2: simulated/recorded conditions, source/T60 variation, MAEE, valid-bin proportion, baselines, and room boundary.

records.eval: The gaze/health system reports an AdaBoost classifier with 0.89 accuracy and 0.67 F1 against a 0.77 baseline after feature selection and k-fold validation. A post-call usability survey contains 39 participants, with 82% reporting high engagement; gaze distance, velocity, saccade, and task metrics are analyzed across cohorts. These are prototype assessment and usability results, not clinical validation.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 5 and Tables 2–3: feature selection, cross-validation, accuracy/F1, cohort analysis, 39-participant survey, and clinical-evidence boundary.

records.eval: Visual-guide audio captioning is evaluated across eight caption metrics under multiple audiovisual shuffle probabilities, with semantic and temporal module ablations, video-length tests, and repeated timed inference. CIDEr, SPICE, and related semantic measures quantify resilience to mismatch while n-gram measures capture reference overlap. Synthetic shuffling and caption proxies do not establish human-level grounding under natural audiovisual errors.
records.evaluation_source: Sections 3–4 and Tables 2–4: shuffle protocol, metric panel, ablations, video-length and timing tests, and mismatch boundary.

records.eval: VetTrain interview data are evaluated with quantitative and qualitative spoken-interaction reasoning tests across language-model families and scales. Prompt ablations add domain knowledge and interaction context, and answer-quality comparisons separate the contribution of each information source; the study is a bounded interview-coaching evaluation rather than a general dialogue benchmark.
records.evaluation_source: Captured Sections 3–5: VetTrain corpus, model/prompt conditions, context and domain-knowledge ablations, and quantitative/qualitative scoring.

records.eval: Human-to-animal and designed-sound voice conversion is compared with conversion baselines using acoustic fidelity measures and listener judgments of plausibility and target-domain identity. The cross-domain source/target set is the denominator; the unusual target sounds test transfer beyond ordinary human speaker pairs, but do not establish broad ecological validity.
records.evaluation_source: Captured evaluation sections: cross-domain source/target conditions, objective audio comparisons, listener protocol, and baseline comparisons.

records.eval: Several text-to-audio models are tested on controlled prompt sets with matched gender-related conditions. A proposed gender-bias score aggregates output attributes across prompts, supplemented by qualitative inspection; the denominator is generated samples per model and prompt group, not a population estimate of social bias.
records.evaluation_source: Captured Sections 3–4: model set, controlled prompts, proposed bias metric, aggregation procedure, and qualitative analysis.

records.eval: Discrete audio representations are compared for automated captioning on Clotho using BLEU, METEOR, ROUGE-L, CIDEr, SPICE, and SPIDEr, with tokenizer and decoder ablations. These reference-caption metrics evaluate agreement with available descriptions and do not directly measure listener grounding.
records.evaluation_source: Captured Sections 4–5: Clotho scope, caption metrics, representation comparisons, decoder conditions, and ablations.

records.eval: Diffusion-based audio captioning is evaluated on captioning benchmarks with quality and diversity metrics, sampling/efficiency comparisons, and ablations of the diffusion conditioning. The reported denominator is benchmark clips and generated samples; diversity is only useful when it remains semantically faithful to the sound.
records.evaluation_source: Captured Sections 4–5: benchmark conditions, caption-quality/diversity metrics, diffusion ablations, and efficiency comparison.

records.eval: The string-quartet separator is tested on a newly created reverberant quartet dataset, including a seating arrangement held out from training. Separation metrics compare the proposed timbral-plus-positional model with state-of-the-art baselines; the held-out seating condition is the key transfer denominator.
records.evaluation_source: Captured Sections 3–5: dataset construction, train/test seating split, reverberant conditions, separation metrics, and baselines.

records.eval: Audiobox TTA-RAG compares retrieval strategies and zero-/few-shot text-to-audio generation on curated evaluation sets with multiple automatic quality metrics and qualitative examples. Top-k retrieval and datastore conditions are ablated; retrieval leakage, curation, and metric validity bound the result.
records.evaluation_source: Captured Sections 4–5: retrieval conditions, zero-/few-shot setup, metric panel, curated test sets, and retrieval ablations.

records.eval: Fault-tolerant 3D localization is evaluated as microphones are removed or corrupted, comparing accuracy and compute as the active array shrinks. Simulated and measured fault conditions test unreliable and unknown-channel cases against localization baselines; room, array, and calibration conditions define the denominator.
records.evaluation_source: Captured Sections 3–5: microphone-count and fault conditions, 3D localization metrics, compute comparison, and baseline protocol.
